procedural_history.impugned_order: Orders passed by the Sub-Divisional Magistrate under s. 18(1) of the Suppression of Immoral Traffic in Women and Girls Act, 1956 with respect to certain premises.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The respondents challenged the validity of section 18 in the Punjab High Court, Circuit Bench at Delhi (Criminal Writs Nos. 3-D, 4-D, 5-D, 6-D, 7-D, 10-D and 12-D of 1962). The High Court held that section 18 violated Article 14 of the Constitution when action is taken independently of s. 7. They allowed the petitions and quashed the notices issued to the respondents and also quashed the order refusing to raise the attachment in respect of flat No. 54.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The first appellant, Shri A. C. Aggarwal, Sub-Divisional Magistrate, Delhi, brought the appeals to the Supreme Court on the strength of certificates issued by the High Court of Punjab. The Supreme Court was approached because the High Court declared s.18 of the Suppression of Immoral Traffic in Women and Girls Act, 1956 as ultra vires Art. 14 of the Constitution.

directions: The learned magistrate is not debarred from taking fresh proceedings against the respondents in accordance with law.

issue.issue_text: Whether Section 18 of the Act is discriminatory and violative of Article 14 of the Constitution.

facts: A Sub-Divisional Magistrate, based on police reports that certain premises were being used as brothels, issued notices under Section 18(1) of the Suppression of Immoral Traffic in Women and Girls Act, 1956.
The occupants of the premises challenged the constitutional validity of Section 18, arguing it violated Article 14.

The High Court agreed with the occupants, holding that Section 18 was ultra vires of the Constitution to the extent that it allowed action to be taken independently of a prosecution under Section 7 of the Act.
law: The respondents argued that Section 18 is discriminatory because it allows for a summary proceeding (a 'hearing' before a magistrate) for conduct that could also be prosecuted under Section 3 or Section 7, which provide the protections of a full criminal trial, including cross-examination and the right to appeal.
They contended that the Act gives the executive an arbitrary choice between two widely different procedures for similarly situated persons, which violates Article 14 of the Constitution.
application: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's reasoning and the respondents' arguments.
The Court held that Section 18 is not discriminatory because it creates a reasonable classification by covering two distinct classes of cases:
1.  **Persons already prosecuted and convicted under Section 3 or 7:** For this group, the proceedings under Section 18 are a consequence of their conviction.

2.  **Persons not yet prosecuted under those sections:** For this group, the proceedings under Section 18 are a preventative measure aimed at stopping the misuse of the premises, rather than a punitive action for a criminal offense.
The Court found that this classification is reasonable and therefore does not violate Article 14.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that Section 18 of the Act is not discriminatory or violative of Article 14 of the Constitution because it provides for two distinct classes of cases, and the classification is reasonable.

issue.issue_text: Whether a magistrate can choose to ignore a cognizable offence disclosed under Section 3 of the Act and instead have recourse only to Section 18, thereby depriving the parties of a regular trial and appeal.

facts: The police submitted reports to a magistrate which disclosed cognizable offenses under Section 3 of the Act against the respondents.
law: Under Section 190(1)(b) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, a magistrate is bound to take cognizance of any cognizable offense brought to their notice.
The Court interpreted the phrase "may take cognizance" in this context to mean "must take cognizance," stating that the magistrate has no discretion in the matter.
The Court reasoned that if a magistrate had discretion to choose between procedures, it would be a violation of Article 14 of the Constitution (equality before the law).
The Act must be given a harmonious construction, meaning its various provisions should be read in a way that makes them work together coherently.
application: The Court applied the principle of harmonious construction to the Act's scheme.
It determined that when a police report discloses a cognizable offense under a penal provision like Section 3, the magistrate must first proceed under that section.
This ensures that the accused person receives the benefit of a regular trial and the right to appeal a conviction.
Only after the case under Section 3 is disposed of can the magistrate then take preventive action under Section 18, if there is a reason to do so.
Therefore, the magistrate cannot simply ignore the criminal offense and choose the summary, preventive procedure under Section 18.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the idea that a magistrate has a choice in such matters. It held that when a report discloses a cognizable offense under Section 3, the magistrate is legally bound to initiate proceedings under that section first. The magistrate cannot ignore the offense and opt for the summary procedure under Section 18, as this would unlawfully deprive the accused of their right to a regular trial and appeal.

issue.issue_text: Whether the set of facts to be proved in prosecutions under Sections 3 or 7 and in proceedings under Section 18 are identical.

law.fact_text: Sections 3 and 7 of the Act are penal provisions that deal with persons guilty of offenses.
Section 18 of the Act is a preventive measure that deals with the premises mentioned therein.

application.fact_text: The Court explained that the sets of facts are not identical because the elements of proof are different.
For a prosecution to succeed under Sections 3 or 7, it must establish the accused's "intention or knowledge."
In contrast, for proceedings under Section 18, intention and knowledge are not necessary ingredients that need to be proven.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that the set of facts to be proved are not identical. The key distinction is that prosecutions under Sections 3 or 7 require proof of the accused's 'intention or knowledge,' while proceedings under Section 18 do not have this requirement.

arguments.issue_text: Whether Section 18 of the Act is discriminatory and violative of Article 14 of the Constitution.
appellant_arguments: Section 18 of the Act is not ultra vires Article 14 of the Constitution.
respondent_arguments: Section 18 discriminates against the parties and is violative of Article 14 of the Constitution.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a magistrate can choose to ignore a cognizable offence disclosed under Section 3 of the Act and instead have recourse only to Section 18, thereby depriving the parties of a regular trial and appeal.
appellant_arguments: The magistrate's action of proceeding under Section 18 was lawful. (Implicit, as the appellant is defending the magistrate's actions which were overturned by the High Court).
respondent_arguments: When reports disclose a cognizable offence under Section 3 of the Act, a magistrate cannot ignore it and merely have recourse to Section 18, as this deprives parties of the benefit of a trial and appeal.
The magistrate is bound to take cognizance of the offence under Section 190(1)(b) of the Code of Criminal Procedure and must first proceed under the penal provisions of Section 3 or 7.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the set of facts to be proved in prosecutions under Sections 3 or 7 and in proceedings under Section 18 are identical.
appellant_arguments: The facts to be proved are not identical, as Section 18 provides for a distinct class of cases, making the classification reasonable. (Implicit in the argument that Section 18 is not discriminatory).
respondent_arguments: The set of facts to be proved are identical, which is why applying a different procedure under Section 18 is discriminatory. (Implicit in the argument that Section 18 violates Article 14).

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A law is not unconstitutional for violating equal protection if its classification is based on a real and substantial distinction that bears a reasonable and just relation to the law's objective. However, even under a constitutionally valid provision, proceedings are not in accordance with the law if a magistrate ignores a disclosed cognizable offense under one section and instead initiates action under a different, subsequent section without first addressing the cognizable offense as required.
obiter: There is a presumption in favor of the constitutionality of an enactment, as it is assumed the legislature understands the needs of its people and bases its laws on experience and adequate grounds.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court holds that the proceedings taken by the magistrate against the respondents are not in accordance with law. When police reports disclose a cognizable offence under Section 3 of the Act, a magistrate cannot ignore that offence and merely have recourse to the preventive measures under Section 18 without first taking action under Section 3.
legal_tests_applied: The inhibition of Art. 14 that the State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws means that there should be no discrimination between one person and another if as regards the subject-matter of the legislation their position is the same.

Reasonable classification is permitted but such classification must be based upon some real and substantial distinction bearing a reasonable and just relation to the thing in respect of which such classification is made.
The presumption is always in favour of the constitutionality of an enactment, since it must be assumed that the legislature understands and correctly appreciates the needs of its own people.
why_appellant_lost: The magistrate's procedure was unlawful because he proceeded against the respondents under Section 18 without first taking action under Section 3, despite the police reports disclosing a cognizable offence.
The magistrate cannot ignore a cognizable offence and merely have recourse to Section 18, as this deprives parties of the benefit of a trial and appeal.
why_respondent_won: The reports submitted by the police disclosed a cognizable offence under Section 3 of the Act.
In such a case, the magistrate cannot ignore the cognizable offence and merely have recourse to Section 18, thus depriving parties of the benefit of a trial and appeal.
The Magistrate should have taken action under Section 190(1)(b) of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
policy_considerations: There is a fundamental distinction between a prosecution and a preventive measure; Sections 3 and 7 provide for the punishment of persons guilty of offences, whereas a proceeding under Section 18 is a preventive measure intended to minimise the chances of a recurrence of the offence.
